facts.statement: Spinops was a medium-sized ceratopsian dinosaur measuring 4.5 meters in length and weighing 1.3 metric tons. (4.5 m, 1.3 MT)
facts.quote: It was a medium-sized ceratopsian, reaching 4.5 m in length and 1.3 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: The holotype of Spinops is a partial parietal bone that preserves most of the midline bar. (NHMUK PV R 16307)
facts.quote: Spinops is known from the holotype NHMUK PV R 16307, a partial parietal bone, preserving most of the midline bar.

facts.statement: Fossils of Spinops were first discovered in 1916 and are housed in the Natural History Museum in London. (1916)
facts.quote: Fossils of Spinops were first found in 1916, and were housed in the Natural History Museum in London.

facts.statement: The fossils were not formally described until 2011, when the species Spinops sternbergorum was named. (2011)
facts.quote: The material was not described until 2011, when the new species Spinops sternbergorum was erected.

facts.statement: Two partial skulls were found in 1916 near the Red Deer River in southern Alberta by collectors Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his son Levi Sternberg. (1916, Red Deer River)
facts.quote: Two partials skulls of Spinops were found in 1916, in a large bone bed near the Red Deer River of southern Alberta, by American commercial fossil collector Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his son Levi Sternberg.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Arthur Smith Woodward initially dismissed the Spinops fossils as "nothing but rubbish". ("nothing but rubbish")
facts.quote: In a letter to Charles H. Sternberg, English paleontologist Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum called the Spinops material "nothing but rubbish".

facts.statement: The genus name Spinops comes from Latin and Greek words meaning "spine" and "face" due to unique facial ornamentation. (spina, ops)
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Latin spina, "spine", and Greek ops, "face", in reference to the unique ornamentation on the face.

facts.statement: Spinops fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous and were likely found in the Oldman or Dinosaur Park Formations. (Campanian, Late Cretaceous)
facts.quote: The material was probably collected from the upper part of the Oldman Formation or the lower part of the Dinosaur Park Formation, dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Spinops lived in North America approximately 76.5 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous. (76.5 millones de años, Campaniense)
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 76.5 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Spinops is classified within the subfamily Centrosaurinae. (Centrosaurinae)
The parent group of the genus Spinops is the tribe Centrosaurini. (Centrosaurini)
Spinops possessed hooks and spines on the back of its frill, making it evolutionarily close to Centrosaurus and Styracosaurus. (ganchos y espinas, Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus)
facts.quote: Spinops tenía ganchos y espinas alrededor de la parte de atrás de su prolongación ósea que hace que se vea evolutivamente un animal próximo a Centrosaurus y Styracosaurus.
